sections.title: 1.1 · Convolutions from scratch
paragraphs: Both implementations compute true convolution: flip the kernel in both dimensions, zero-pad the image, and accumulate products. The four-loop version iterates over image rows, image columns, kernel rows, and kernel columns. The two-loop version keeps the two kernel loops and multiplies a whole shifted image slice at once. No convolution routine, FFT, window-view helper, or image-processing library is used inside either implementation.

For a kernel of height Kh and width Kw, padding before each axis is floor(K/2) and padding after it is floor((K−1)/2). This asymmetry for even kernels matches SciPy’s “same” crop convention. Testing non-symmetric odd and even kernels is necessary: a symmetric Gaussian alone would not catch an accidental correlation or a one-pixel offset.

The grayscale selfie is 384 × 512 pixels; luminance uses 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B on RGB values in [0,1]. The 9 × 9 average removes fine texture. Dₓ and Dᵧ emphasize changes across columns and rows respectively; the signed display has one common symmetric color scale. Zero extension visibly darkens a smoothed outer rim and can introduce false derivatives at the frame.

For a fixed 96 × 96 selfie crop/resize, the table reports the median of three timed calls after one warm-up. Every method uses float64, zero extension, and “same” output. Maximum error across all comparisons is 8.88e-16. These are measurements on this computer, not universal speed claims. Both manual methods do O(HWKhKw) arithmetic; vectorizing the image operations removes Python’s per-pixel overhead.

The boundary test uses an all-ones 25 × 25 image and a normalized 9 × 9 box. Zero fill produces 25/81 at a corner and 5/9 along an edge; symmetric and periodic extension preserve one everywhere. “Same” describes output size, not how pixels beyond the image are supplied.

code.title: Input validation, kernel flip, and exact padding
code.text:
def _convolution_inputs(image, kernel):
    image = np.asarray(image, dtype=np.float64)
    kernel = np.asarray(kernel, dtype=np.float64)
    if image.ndim != 2 or kernel.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("image and kernel must both be two dimensional")
    if not image.size or not kernel.size:
        raise ValueError("image and kernel must be nonempty")
    kh, kw = kernel.shape
    # Before = ceil((K-1)/2); after = floor((K-1)/2).
    padded = np.pad(image, ((kh // 2, (kh - 1) // 2),
                            (kw // 2, (kw - 1) // 2)), mode='constant')
    return image, kernel[::-1, ::-1], padded

sections.title: 1.2 · Finite difference operator
paragraphs: The horizontal and vertical responses are gx = I ∗ [1,0,−1] and gy = I ∗ [1,0,−1]ᵀ. True convolution flips the stencil, so a left-to-right brightening gives positive gx. Gradient magnitude is √(gx² + gy²); it combines both directions into an unsigned edge-strength map.

The supplied public cameraman rendering has a thin white border. I crop it to (1, 7, 535, 541) (left, top, right, bottom; right/bottom excluded), then resize the remaining square to 256 × 256 with Lanczos. All calculations use floating intensities in [0,1], with no per-image normalization before thresholding.

I compare thresholds 0.08, 0.16, and 0.24, which retain 23.7%, 12.8%, and 9.0% of the evaluated interior. I choose 0.16: it retains the person, camera, and tripod more clearly than 0.24 while rejecting much of the ground texture retained by 0.08. This is a visual tradeoff, not an accuracy score against annotated ground truth.

The edge predicate is magnitude > T. A seven-pixel frame is excluded from binary maps and edge-fraction measurements throughout Part 1, preventing zero-padding artifacts from being mistaken for scene edges and matching the largest Gaussian derivative support used below. The signed derivative and magnitude images still show their unmasked responses.

sections.title: 1.3 · Derivative of Gaussian
paragraphs: I construct a 13 × 13 Gaussian at σ = 2 pixels as the outer product of cv2.getGaussianKernel(13,2) with itself. First blur with G, then differentiate with Dₓ/Dᵧ. Equivalently, form Kx = G ∗ Dₓ and Ky = G ∗ Dᵧ once, then use a single convolution per derivative. These are finite-difference derivatives of the sampled Gaussian; their supports are 13 × 15 and 15 × 13 because full kernel convolution preserves the extra two samples.

Convolution associativity gives I ∗ (G ∗ D) = (I ∗ G) ∗ D on the same zero-extended infinite image. In a finite implementation, calling “same” after BOTH stages throws away the blurred halo and breaks equality at the frame: the maximum error here is 0.307, although the evaluated interior agrees to 8.95e-16. Retaining the full Gaussian result, applying the derivative, and cropping only once restores agreement over the entire image to 8.95e-16. The discrepancy panel makes this boundary issue explicit.

Compared with raw finite differences, DoG removes fine grass texture and yields smoother, wider contours. It can merge nearby edges and remove weak detail; Gaussian smoothing is therefore a noise/detail tradeoff. I use T = 0.08 for DoG and T = 0.16 for raw gradients because smoothing lowers response amplitudes. These are separately chosen operating points, not proof that one detector has higher accuracy.

To test noise sensitivity, I add seeded Gaussian noise with σ = 0.08 and clip to [0,1]. I compare each noisy gradient with its own clean counterpart, avoiding the mistake of calling intentional smoothing a noise error. Interior vector-gradient residual RMS falls from 0.15226 for finite differences to 0.01030 for DoG (14.8× lower). This measures stability for this image/noise realization, not recovery of lost detail.

sections.title: Mandatory extension · Gradient orientations
paragraphs: The orientation implementation calls no arctangent, atan2, or angle routine. It takes r = min(|gy|,|gx|)/max(|gy|,|gx|), then range-reduces r above √2−1 using atan(r) = π/4 + atan((r−1)/(r+1)). The reduced argument has magnitude at most √2−1, so 18 terms of z − z³/3 + z⁵/5 − … converge accurately. Coordinate swaps and component signs restore all four quadrants; a zero gradient is assigned angle zero and displayed black.

Hue is θ mod 2π divided by 2π; saturation is one. Value is min(magnitude / p99.5, 1)^0.7, with p99.5 = 0.2386, so stronger gradients appear brighter and faint background responses remain subdued. The colors represent directed intensity change, not the tangent direction of the edge. Since image rows increase downward, 90° points down. NumPy atan2 is used only as an independent validation reference: maximum angular error on this figure is 4.44e-16 radians.

figures.caption: HSV orientation visualization computed without built-in angle functions. Direction follows image coordinates; the seven-pixel border is excluded.
figures.alt: HSV orientation visualization computed without built-in angle functions. Direction follows image coordinates; the seven-pixel border is excluded.

code.title: Arithmetic-only orientation implementation
code.text:
def orientation_without_angles(gx, gy, terms=18):
    """Quadrant-correct atan2 equivalent using arithmetic and a Taylor series.

    No arctan/arctan2/angle function is used. Range reduction first replaces
    the ratio by min(|y|,|x|)/max(|y|,|x|), then uses
      atan(r) = pi/4 + atan((r-1)/(r+1)) for r > tan(pi/8).
    This bounds the series argument by sqrt(2)-1, giving fast convergence.
    At a zero gradient the angle is assigned zero (orientation is undefined).
    Signed-zero distinctions on the negative x-axis are immaterial for hue.
    """
    gx, gy = np.broadcast_arrays(np.asarray(gx, float), np.asarray(gy, float))
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(gx)) or not np.all(np.isfinite(gy)):
        raise ValueError('gradient components must be finite')
    if terms < 1:
        raise ValueError('terms must be positive')
    ax, ay = np.abs(gx), np.abs(gy)
    high, low = np.maximum(ax, ay), np.minimum(ax, ay)
    ratio = np.divide(low, high, out=np.zeros_like(high), where=high != 0)
    reduce = ratio > np.sqrt(2.0) - 1.0
    z = np.where(reduce, (ratio - 1.0) / (ratio + 1.0), ratio)
    # Horner evaluation of z - z^3/3 + z^5/5 - ... .
    z2 = z * z
    poly = np.zeros_like(z)
    for n in range(terms - 1, -1, -1):
        poly = ((-1.0) ** n) / (2 * n + 1) + z2 * poly
    small_angle = z * poly + np.where(reduce, np.pi / 4, 0.0)
    angle = np.where(ay > ax, np.pi / 2 - small_angle, small_angle)
    angle = np.where(gx < 0, np.pi - angle, angle)
    angle = np.where(gy < 0, -angle, angle)
    return np.where(high == 0, 0.0, angle)

sections.title: 2.1 · Image sharpening
paragraphs: Let B = G ∗ I be the low-pass image and H = I − B its high-frequency residual. Unsharp masking forms S = I + αH = (1 + α)I − α(G ∗ I). Since I = δ ∗ I and convolution is linear, one convolution suffices: S = [(1 + α)δ − αG] ∗ I. The kernel has unit sum, so a constant image is preserved when the boundary extension also preserves constants.

I use a 13 × 13 Gaussian at σ = 2 pixels, symmetric boundaries to avoid dark zero-padded borders, and independent float64 RGB-channel processing. All computation keeps signed residuals and unclipped sharpened values until display/export. The figures include the Taj Mahal, an additional original street photograph, and α = 0.5, 1, 2. Increasing α strengthens existing edges and texture but also amplifies noise, halos, and values outside the display range.

The single-convolution expression agrees with I + α(I − G∗I) at α = 1 to a maximum error of 1.78e-15 over these images. High-frequency residuals are displayed as 0.5 + 2H, where middle gray means zero; they are not independently normalized. The clipped-sample table counts RGB channel values outside [0,1] before clipping, exposing a cost hidden by an attractive display.

For the recovery experiment, I deliberately blur the original street image once, then sharpen that blurred image with the same Gaussian at each tested α. The best tested display result is α = 2: clipped RGB MSE changes from 0.001660 after blur to 0.001099 after sharpening, and PSNR changes from 27.80 to 29.59 dB. The parameter was selected against this reference and is not a general optimum.

Resharpening makes blurred transitions steeper but does not restore all original detail. If the blur transfer is G(f), the blur-then-unsharp transfer is G(f)[1 + α − αG(f)], which is generally not one. Frequencies reduced nearly to zero cannot be reconstructed by this finite boost, and clipping can discard additional information. The crop, residual map, and nonzero MSE support this limitation; perceptual crispness alone does not establish recovery.

sections.title: 2.2 · Hybrid images
paragraphs: A hybrid adds a blurred source to detail from a second aligned source: H = G_sigmaL * A + gain (B - G_sigmaH * B). Here the people provide the low-frequency image and the cats provide the high-frequency image. The three required examples are Derek + Nutmeg and two custom portrait/cat pairs.

I aligned the eye centers with a two-point similarity transform before filtering. The transform permits rotation, uniform scale and translation, but no face warping. The existing landmarks line up the pupils well, so the refinement changes the frequency separation and gain. Full original coordinates and 2 x 3 transforms are saved with the results.

The initial sigma-low 10, sigma-high 5, gain 1 settings left substantial cat shading at reduced sizes. Moving the high-pass sigma to 1.5 removes more of that broad structure. A gain of 2.2–3 restores fine fur contrast, while sigma-low 6 retains enough human eye and mouth structure to read at smaller sizes. The selected gain is lower for the dense tabby texture than for the lighter portrait cat. These are judgments from the displayed comparisons, not a universally optimal setting.

In the selected astronaut example, the 512-pixel view emphasizes cat fur and eye rims; the astronaut eyes and smile are readable at 128 pixels and clearer at 64. The 256-pixel view still contains both identities. Increasing gain further strengthens fine edges but also clips more highlights; increasing sigma-high leaks broader cat structure back into the reduced view. The six actual trials expose these tradeoffs.

To view the effect, open the largest result at normal size, then increase your viewing distance or compare the smaller versions. Keep the displayed image fixed while moving back. Exact distances depend on screen size, zoom and eyesight, so the pixel-size sequence is a repeatable demonstration rather than a calibrated distance test.

The Gaussian has no sharp cutoff. Its approximate half-amplitude frequency is sqrt(2 ln 2) / (2 pi sigma) cycles per output pixel. For the selected astronaut pair this is 0.0312 for the low pass and 0.1249 for the complementary high pass. The filtering itself is spatial convolution; the Fourier plots diagnose the resulting bands.

All filtering and addition use signed float64 values. Display exports clamp to [0,1] and quantize to 8 bits; the table reports the fraction of scalar channel values clipped. No intermediate band is clipped or contrast-normalized during synthesis. Additional alignment/component views, all other trial grids and the unsuccessful Earth + Moon study are included as supplemental figures.

sections.title: Color · Which frequency band benefits?
paragraphs: The four controlled variants put color in neither source, only the low-frequency source, only the high-frequency source, or both. Low-only color preserves broad skin and hair hues associated with the distant astronaut. High-only color contributes colored fine edges but cannot recover the cat’s broad coat color after that information has been removed.

For this pair, low-only color is the most coherent color version: its large color regions agree with the distant face, while grayscale fur remains visible nearby. Both-color adds localized competing hues around some cat edges. The grayscale main examples make the frequency-dependent identity easier to judge without a broad color cue.

figures.caption: The four variants use identical geometry, sigma values and detail gain. Only conversion to luminance changes (weights 0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722). Broad human skin and hair colors survive the low pass; high-only color is confined to edges and fine cat detail.

sections.title: 2.3 · Gaussian and Laplacian stacks
paragraphs: The apple and orange are the supplied course originals, burt_apple.png and burt_orange.png. Each 740 x 530 input is resized once to 512 x 367 pixels with area interpolation, retaining its aspect ratio to the nearest output pixel. This common working size keeps the experiment efficient without stretching the fruit into a square.

A stack keeps every level at full resolution. I set G0 = I, then blur the original independently at sigma = 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 pixels. The detail bands are Li = Gi - G(i+1) for i = 0,...,4; L5 = G5 is the coarse residual. Independent blurring makes the effective sigma of each level explicit. No downsampling occurs between stack levels, and no built-in pyramid routine is used.

The residual is essential: summing only the detail bands would recover I - G5 and lose the large-scale brightness and color. With the residual, the sum telescopes exactly to I up to floating-point rounding. The apple and orange reconstruction errors are reported below.

The mask follows the same Gaussian schedule. Each output level is Si = Mi LAi + (1 - Mi) LBi, including the residual level, and the final image is the sum of all Si. A is selected wherever the initial mask is white. This separates fine texture transitions from broad illumination and color transitions.

figures.caption: Apple: full-resolution Gaussian stack (top) and Laplacian stack (bottom), including the coarse residual. All six arrays preserve the working resolution of 512 x 367 pixels (width x height). Signed bands use 0.5 + 2.5L for display; the residual uses its actual intensity.

Orange: full-resolution Gaussian stack (top) and Laplacian stack (bottom), including the coarse residual. All six arrays preserve the working resolution of 512 x 367 pixels (width x height). Signed bands use 0.5 + 2.5L for display; the residual uses its actual intensity.

The binary left/right mask is blurred at exactly the Gaussian image-stack scales. Fine bands use a sharp transition; coarser bands mix over progressively wider neighborhoods. White selects apple, black selects orange.

Reproduction of the Figure 3.42 (a)–(l) layout: rows 1–3 show levels 0, 2 and 4, with masked apple, masked orange and their sum in the three columns. Row 4 reconstructs each contribution and the final oraple by summing ALL five detail bands plus the coarse residual. Detail displays share a symmetric contrast scale across each row; row 4 is shown in actual [0,1] intensity.

G = [I] + [gaussian(I, 2 * 2**i) for i in range(5)]
L = [G[i] - G[i+1] for i in range(5)] + [G[-1]]
S = [M[i] * LA[i] + (1-M[i]) * LB[i] for i in range(6)]
result = sum(S)

sections.title: 2.4 · Multiresolution blending
paragraphs: The standard apple/orange blend uses the apple on the left and the orange on the right. A direct binary cut preserves a conspicuous vertical brightness/color discontinuity; mixing corresponding Laplacian bands with Gaussian mask weights spreads that transition according to scale while retaining local texture.

For these inputs, the mean absolute RGB difference across the two columns adjoining the seam decreases from 0.1716 to 0.0279. This local diagnostic supports the visible seam comparison; it is not a general perceptual-quality score.

The seam measurement is computed on the unclipped floating-point reconstruction. For display export only, values are clamped to [0,1]; 2.35% of scalar RGB values require this clamp. No clipping occurs within the stack or before reconstruction.

figures.caption: Course-provided inputs, selection mask, hard-cut baseline and full-color multiresolution oraple. Both baselines use the same aspect-preserving 512 x 367 input images and the same initial mask; the seam is between columns 255 and 256 (zero-based).

sections.title: Two custom color blends · Irregular selections
paragraphs: Tabby disguise transfers the tabby’s central face onto the orange-and-white cat while retaining the destination’s ears, whiskers and chest. An irregular 18-vertex polygon follows the forehead and cheeks. Eye-center alignment puts the face texture in a plausible position. The hard cut exposes the polygon immediately; multiscale blending softens the coat-color transition while keeping the transferred eyes and fur crisp.

One world, two surfaces is an imaginary globe: Earth’s oceans and clouds transition into lunar craters along an S-shaped boundary. Ellipses fitted to the largest source contours above luminance 0.04 are mapped to a shared circle. This affine registration corrects approximately 1% anisotropy in the photographed Earth outline; the Moon needs almost uniform scaling. Thresholding only measures geometry and does not mask or recolor either photograph. Their shared round outline supports this composite even though their textures did not produce a convincing frequency-switching hybrid. This is an artistic surface fusion, not an astronomical depiction.

Both examples use the entire registered source photographs. The background is never copied into the other source before filtering. Hard cut, single-scale feathering and multiscale blending receive identical arrays and the same underlying binary selection. The feather baseline uses the exact coarsest stack mask on the full images: its wide transition mixes competing fine details as well as broad colors.

The globe initially showed a small notch where its seam met the silhouette: a binary mask still switched the finest detail band abruptly between different limb contrasts. I tested initial-mask Gaussian widths of 0, 2, 4, 8, 12 and 16 pixels. Sigma 8 is the smallest tested width that makes the join continuous without unnecessarily widening the texture mixture. Only the selection weights change; the source photographs and image bands remain sharp. The Gaussian mask stack starts from this softened selection, giving nominal widths of 8, 8.2, 8.9, 11.3, 17.9, 33.0 and 64.5 pixels. The cat and canonical oraple retain their binary finest masks. The controlled lower-limb sweep is in the supplement.

The cat uses five detail bands (sigma = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 pixels); the globe uses six (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 pixels). Both retain their coarse residual. Supplementary sweeps test four, five and six bands without changing other inputs. For the cat, 16 pixels leaves a more conspicuous facial patch; 32 softens the coat boundary without the broader tonal spill of 64. The globe benefits from 64 pixels because its brightness mismatch spans a large fraction of the disk.

Compared with broad feathering, the cat’s cheek and muzzle retain more definite tabby detail; feathering mixes both faces over a broad transition. At the globe’s boundary, clouds and crater detail remain more localized in the multiscale result. The boundary-jump values below measure adjacent RGB differences across the original binary contour. Feathering gives still smaller jumps because it mixes more image detail; minimizing this number would not select the most convincing photograph. It is a local seam diagnostic, not a perceptual score or proof of physical realism.

Color helps both concepts. The warm tabby patch remains distinct from white fur and orange ears; grayscale makes these coat regions less distinct. The globe’s blue oceans contrast with the nearly neutral Moon and make the two surfaces easier to identify. I prefer RGB for the final composites; grayscale controls show that seam smoothing also works without this color cue.

Multiresolution blending cannot fix anatomical or surface mismatches. The cats still differ slightly in muzzle shape and fur direction, and lunar features cannot continue Earth’s clouds naturally. Smoothing the finest mask removes the abrupt limb join, but does not make this imaginary surface physically continuous. Processing stays signed float64; only final image display is clipped to [0,1].

hybrids.title: Derek + Nutmeg
hybrids.selection_note: A narrow high-pass band retains whiskers nearby while reducing broad cat shading at smaller scales. Gain 2.5 keeps this detail visible; the distant face remains somewhat mixed at 128 pixels.

hybrids.title: Astronaut + portrait cat

hybrids.title: Obama + tabby
